old_entry.title: Atari Video Computer System
old_entry.subtitle: A library in cartridges
old_entry.summary: The console later called the Atari 2600 made a changing software collection part of home life.
body: Atari released its Video Computer System in 1977. Its cartridge library eventually ranged from arcade conversions to original adventures and experiments. Distinctive controllers, a wood-grain front and game boxes turned computer entertainment into a recognisable household product.

Creating for the machine demanded precise control of limited memory and display timing. Its constraints helped produce a visual vocabulary of strong silhouettes, flat colour and repeated patterns that remains readable decades later.

editorial_features.title: Learning the new box
editorial_features.summary: Manuals teach a household to play.
body: The Atari VCS owner's booklet begins before any game can start. Its diagrams address different television antenna connections, explain the TV/Game switch box and show where the controllers belong. The household television was existing equipment with its own fittings and habits. Buying a console did not replace that arrangement; it added another use that had to be connected and later switched away. The drawings turn installation into a sequence a household can follow. Their prominence shows how much instruction belonged outside the game program itself.

Once a cartridge was inserted with the power off, more choices remained. Atari's booklet explains a numbered Game Select display, separate difficulty switches for the two players and a reset switch that starts the chosen game. It sends the owner back to the individual game's instructions for what those settings mean. The console supplied a common vocabulary of controls, while each cartridge interpreted it. A box that could host different games therefore needed a continuing partnership between its physical switches, the screen and the paper placed beside it.

Fairchild's 1976 booklet calls the console programmable, but its opening examples make that word concrete. For the built-in Hockey game, numbered buttons answer on-screen prompts about the game, time limit and speed. An owner can accept defaults or select options before starting. This is programming as the booklet presents it to a player: configuring an activity through a controlled conversation with the machine. It does not mean that every buyer is writing software. The distinction helps recover what a flexible game system actually offered within an ordinary evening.

The Fairchild controller also changes meaning with the activity. In Hockey, the booklet maps movement, twisting and vertical knob action to players and goalie, with diagrams explaining how these motions can combine. Optional Videocart software extends the system beyond its built-in Hockey and Tennis. The hand stays around the same object while the instructions change what that object does. Comparing the two manufacturers' booklets makes interchangeability tangible: a continuing household device, new rules arriving with software, and people learning how to connect the two.

images.context_review_note: The actual first-model hardware visibly labels RESET, buttons1–4, HOCKEY/TENNIS/GAME3/GAME4, TIME2/5/10/20MIN and MODE/HOLD/START.
